args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION/ARBITRATION

MEMORANDUM

TO:      Engagement Team
FROM:    Arbitration & International Dispute Resolution Group
DATE:    [Current Date]
RE:      Analysis of Counterparty Markup of Arbitration Agreement
         Accept / Reject / Counter Recommendation Memorandum
FILE:    arbitration-international-dispute-resolution — Counterparty Markup Analysis

I.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have reviewed the counterparty's redline markup of the arbitration agreement against
(i) our original draft, (ii) the operative excerpts of the Stock Purchase Agreement ("SPA")
into which the arbitration clause is to be incorporated, and (iii) our internal playbook on
international arbitration provisions and firm precedent. The counterparty's markup introduces
a series of substantive deviations across the scope of arbitrability, seat/venue, governing law,
consolidation, the appointment of arbitrators, discovery scope, interim relief, costs and fee
shifting, confidentiality, and the enforceability of the award.

On balance, a substantial majority of the counterparty's changes are commercially
unacceptable and should be rejected, and most of the remainder warrant counterproposals that
preserve our client's key litigation and enforcement protections. We recommend a disciplined
negotiating posture: (1) accept the handful of changes that genuinely align with market practice
and do not prejudice our client; (2) reject, with brief reasoning, the changes that deviate from
firm precedent in ways that would disadvantage our client; and (3) advance targeted counter-
language where a middle position is commercially defensible.

II.    BACKGROUND AND DOCUMENTS REVIEWED

A.     Original Draft
Our firm's original draft arbitration agreement, prepared in accordance with the internal
international arbitration playbook and firm precedent, contains the following core architecture:
(i) a broad arbitration clause covering all disputes "arising out of or relating to" the SPA and
the transactions contemplated thereby; (ii) a designated seat and governing law; (iii) a
specified arbitral institution and rules; (iv) a three-member tribunal with an appointment
mechanism; (v) a broad discovery provision; (vi) the availability of interim and injunctive
relief; and (vii) allocation of costs and fees consistent with default institutional rules.

B.     Counterparty Redline
The counterparty's markup (the "Redline") revises the agreement across each of the principal
provisions. The deviations are catalogued and analyzed in Section IV below.

C.     SPA Excerpts
The arbitration agreement is to be executed as a schedule/exhibit to the SPA. Relevant SPA
terms—most importantly the governing law, jurisdiction, definitions of "Dispute," and the
indemnification/limitation-of-liability framework—created anchor points that the arbitration
provision must respect to maintain internal consistency.

D.     Internal Playbook & Firm Precedent
Our internal playbook prescribes baseline positions for international arbitration provisions:
neutral and pro-enforcement forum selection, well-established rules, balanced arbitrator
appointment, proportionate discovery, preservation of equitable relief, and cost allocation that
does not discourage legitimate claims. The Redline is evaluated against those baselines below.

E.     Practice Area Parameters
This matter falls within arbitration and international dispute resolution. The analysis that
follows applies generally accepted principles of international commercial arbitration,
including enforceability under the New York Convention, institutional rules, and prevailing
market practice for cross-border M&A disputes.

III.   GOVERNING FRAMEWORK

Three considerations drive our assessment of each markup item:

1.    Enforceability. Any agreed language must yield an award enforceable under the New
      York Convention and, where applicable, the governing lex arbitri. Language that
      undermines valid consent to arbitrate, imposes forum-selection limitations that invite
      non-arbitrability challenges, or creates ambiguity as to tribunal authority should be
      resisted.
2.    Client Interest. Each provision must be evaluated for how it shifts litigation risk, cost,
      procedural leverage, and enforceability in favor of or against our client, who in this
      matter expects efficient resolution without sacrificing access to full remedial relief.
3.    Market Practice. Provisions should be measured against prevailing market norms for
      comparable cross-border M&A transaction arbitration clauses. Where the Redline
      departs from market practice to the counterparty's unilateral advantage, we treat it as
      a markup to be rejected or countered.

IV.    DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS

Set out below is our assessment of each deviation introduced by the counterparty in the
Redline, with a recommendation of Accept, Reject, or Counter.

1.    Scope of Arbitrability — Narrowing to "Arising Under" Only

      Redline: Removes "or relating to" and limits submission to disputes "arising directly
      under" the SPA.

      Analysis: The deletion of "relating to" materially narrows the breadth of the arbitration
      clause, excluding related disputes (e.g., tort, misrepresentation, and collateral claims)
      that would otherwise be swept into arbitration. This invites parallel litigation over
      related claims, undermining the efficiency and cost-containment objectives of a
      mandatory arbitration program. It also increases the risk of inconsistent findings on
      overlapping facts. This is a classic deviation from market practice, which generally
      favors a broad clause.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Restore the broad "arising out of or relating to" language,
      consistent with firm precedent.

2.    Seat of Arbitration — Change of Default Seat

      Redline: Proposes moving the seat from a neutral, established arbitral seat to the
      counterparty's home jurisdiction.

      Analysis: Selection of seat determines the procedural law governing the arbitration and
      the venue for challenge/enforcement of the award. Moving the seat to the counterparty's
      home jurisdiction confers a home-court advantage in applications to set aside the award
      and increases the practical burden on our client. It also risks perceptions of bias and may
      complicate enforcement. Deviates from the playbook's preference for a neutral seat.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Maintain our designated neutral seat.

3.    Governing Law — Unilateral Selection

      Redline: Selects the counterparty's domestic law as governing law for the arbitration
      agreement and the underlying SPA carve-outs.

      Analysis: Governing law affects interpretation, validity, and enforceability of the
      arbitration agreement itself. A unilateral choice favoring the counterparty's law, without
      corresponding benefit to our client, is not balanced and is contrary to the playbook.
      Proper and balanced governing law is central to predictability of the arbitral process.

      Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER. Propose mutually-agreed governing law (or
      retain the SPA's governing law), rather than the counterparty's unilateral choice.

4.    Arbitral Institution / Rules — Shift to a Less Established Institution

      Redline: Substitutes a less established institution and its rules for the well-recognized
      institution in our original draft.

      Analysis: Well-established institutions (e.g., ICC, HKIAC, SIAC, LCIA) are preferred
      for their procedural certainty, quality of administration, and enforceability track record.
      Substituting a less established institution increases administrative uncertainty and could
      complicate the process. Deviates from firm precedent.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Retain the originally designated institution.

5.    Number of Arbitrators — Reduction to Sole Arbitrator

      Redline: Changes the tribunal from three arbitrators to a sole arbitrator.

      Analysis: A sole arbitrator reduces cost but concentrates decision-making authority in
      a single individual and, for disputes of the magnitude contemplated by this transaction,
      may be undesirable. The playbook generally favors a three-member panel for larger
      matters; however, a sole arbitrator may be a commercially acceptable trade given
      expediency and cost savings, provided the appointment mechanism is balanced.

      Recommendation: COUNTER. We are open to a sole arbitrator in exchange for balanced
      appointment and other concessions on enforceability provisions.

6.    Appointment/Challenge Mechanism — Counterparty Control

      Redline: Grants the counterparty or its designee increased control over the appointment
      and challenge of arbitrators, including a unilateral appointment right.

      Analysis: A balanced appointment mechanism is essential to a fair and reliable tribunal.
      Unilateral appointment control impermissibly advantages the counterparty and invites
      challenges to the tribunal's legitimacy and the enforceability of the award. Deviates
      sharply from the playbook.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Adopt the institution's standard, balanced appointment and
      challenge process.

7.    Discovery Scope — Elimination of Document Production

      Redline: Deletes the document production/discovery provision.

      Analysis: Contractual discovery and document production are important tools in
      international arbitration for fact development. Eliminating them entirely would
      constrain our client's ability to prove claims and defenses and is not standard market
      practice for disputes of this size. It asymmetrically benefits the counterparty if it is the
      likely respondent holding the relevant documents.

      Recommendation: COUNTER. Preserve reasonable, proportionate document production
      consistent with the applicable rules and IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence.

8.    Interim and Injunctive Relief — Foreclosure of Equitable Relief

      Redline: Attempts to preclude the tribunal from granting interim, provisional, or
      injunctive relief, or subordinates such relief to pre-arbitral court proceedings.

      Analysis: The availability of interim and injunctive relief is a critical protection,
      particularly in M&A disputes involving ongoing conduct and preservation of the status
      quo. Foreclosing or unduly restricting equitable relief is contrary to market practice and
      the playbook and could seriously harm our client's ability to protect its position pending
      a final award.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Preserve the tribunal's authority to order interim and
      injunctive relief and the parties' right to seek urgent relief from courts where necessary.

9.    Consolidation / Joinder — Broad Unilateral Right

      Redline: Adds a broad right of consolidation and joinder available to the counterparty.

      Analysis: Consolidation and joinder can be efficient in related disputes, but a broad
      unilateral right in favor of the counterparty risks dragging unrelated parties/claims into
      a single forum to our client's disadvantage. Market practice typically conditions
      consolidation on consent or on closely-related disputes.

      Recommendation: COUNTER. Limit consolidation/joinder to closely-related disputes
      and require mutual consent or tribunal approval.

10.   Costs / Fee Shifting — Loser-Pays Asymmetry

      Redline: Introduces a cost and fee-shifting provision that is asymmetric or that shifts
      costs only against our client, and/or imposes caps on recovery of fees.

      Analysis: Cost allocation that operates only against one party is contrary to market
      practice and discourages the legitimate pursuit of claims. The playbook supports cost
      allocation that follows the applicable institutional rules and is neutral in application.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Restore neutral cost-allocation language consistent with the
      governing institutional rules.

11.   Confidentiality — Asymmetric Obligations

      Redline: Imposes confidentiality obligations principally on our client while exempting
      the counterparty and its affiliates.

      Analysis: Confidentiality in arbitration protects commercially sensitive information. An
      asymmetric confidentiality regime, shielding the counterparty but burdening our client,
      is not acceptable and is contrary to the balanced approach in the playbook.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Adopt mutual, balanced confidentiality terms.

12.   Finality / Waiver of Appeal — Waiver Limitations

      Redline: Modifies the waiver of appeal and finality provisions to preserve broad appeal
      or vacatur rights that could be used to delay enforcement.

      Analysis: The finality of arbitral awards and waiver of merits-based appeal are central
      to the utility of arbitration and to expedited enforcement under the New York
      Convention. Preserving broad basis for challenge undermines finality and invites
      delay.

      Recommendation: REJECT. Retain standard finality and waiver of merits appeal
      language.

13.   Conditions / Indemnification Interface — Conformity to SPA

      Redline: Aligns the arbitration clause carve-outs with the SPA's indemnification and
      limitation-of-liability provisions in a manner that excludes our client's most valuable
      claims from arbitration.

      Analysis: The interface between the dispute-resolution clause and the SPA's
      indemnification framework must preserve the client's full remedial rights while staying
      internally consistent. Excluding valuable claims from the arbitrable universe is
      unacceptable.

      Recommendation: COUNTER. Conform the arbitration scope to the SPA's full
      indemnification framework without carving out the client's material claims.

V.     SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS

      DEVIATION                                        RECOMMENDATION
      -------------------------------------------------------------
      1. Narrowed scope ("arising under")              REJECT
      2. Change of seat to counterparty's home         REJECT
      3. Unilateral governing law                       REJECT / COUNTER
      4. Less established institution/rules             REJECT
      5. Reduction to sole arbitrator                   COUNTER
      6. Unilateral appointment/challenge               REJECT
      7. Elimination of discovery                       COUNTER
      8. Foreclosure of interim/injunctive relief       REJECT
      9. Unilateral consolidation/joinder               COUNTER
      10. Asymmetric cost/fee shifting                  REJECT
      11. Asymmetric confidentiality                    REJECT
      12. Restricted finality/waiver                    REJECT
      13. SPA carve-outs excluding claims               COUNTER

      Net posture: Of the thirteen deviations examined, seven are recommended for
      outright rejection, four warrant counterproposals, and two are hybrids where a counter
      may be defensible. We find no deviation that we recommend accepting as-is; the
      closest candidate (the sole-arbitrator change) should only be accepted as part of a
      broader negotiated package.

VI.   RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATING STRATEGY

1.    Anchor on Market Practice. Open the negotiation by reinforcing the broad clauses
      (scope, seat, governing law, institution, equitable relief) that reflect firm precedent
      and market practice, framing the counterparty's deviations as outliers.

2.    Offer Targeted Concessions. Where we have recommended "Counter," identify
      acceptable middle ground (e.g., sole arbitrator, limited consolidation) that the
      counterparty can claim as a win without eroding core protections, and use these as
      currency to secure acceptance of the broad scope and enforceability provisions.

3.    Maintain Red Lines. Reject, without substantive concession, the changes that strike
      at enforceability (seat, governing law, appointment control, finality, interim relief), as
      any compromise on these would materially harm the client's position in a future
      arbitration.

4.    Preserve Internal Consistency. Ensure the final arbitration provision remains
      internally consistent with the SPA's governing law, jurisdiction, and indemnification
      architecture, so that no conflicting forum-selection or carve-out ambiguity is created.

VII.  CONCLUSION

The counterparty's redline, taken as a whole, seeks to shift significant procedural and
enforcement leverage to its advantage across nearly every core provision of the arbitration
agreement. We recommend a disciplined approach: reject the enforceability-critical changes,
counter the commercially-negotiable items, and resist any concession that undermines the
efficiency, neutrality, and enforceability of the arbitral forum. If adopted with our
recommended revisions, the arbitration agreement will preserve the client's access to full,
efficient, and enforceable dispute resolution.

Please do not hesitate to reach out if you would like to discuss any of the recommended
positions or the negotiation strategy in further detail.

[Prepared for the engagement team by the Arbitration & International Dispute Resolution
Group. Privileged and confidential — attorney work product prepared in anticipation of
arbitration/litigation. Not for disclosure outside the engagement team.]
